question.title: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "Some know-it-alls claim that AI is too big to fail. What do you think about this?", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

answer.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "I think that statement is too stupid to even merit a rebuttal, that\u2019s what I think.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The AI bubble is, like absolutely every other bubble through history, built upon the assumption that there will be cartloads of money coming in at some point in the future.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The verdict is in now: AI slop can\u2019t be sold. At any price. It\u2019s worthless.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "And if you think about it, this is 100% rational behaviour by consumers. If it\u2019s done with AI, no skill, effort, or actual work went into it. The consumer can make it themselves with minimal effort. Why pay for it? Especially since in most cases, anyone can see that it was made by AI. If you can\u2019t see it immediately, you can see it when you try to use the product, which is almost invariably of low quality.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "I mean, AI art is much, much better than what I can produce myself, because I\u2019m not actually an artist. It\u2019s crap compared to what an actual artist can produce.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Witness, for instance, AI music. Some ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "33% of everything that\u2019s uploaded to Spotify today is AI-generated", "modifiers": {"bold": true}}, {"text": ".", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Success story? No. ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "It accounts for 0.5% of all streams", "modifiers": {"bold": true}}, {"text": ". It\u2019s a massive failure. It hogs bandwidth and storage space, and ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "no one wants to listen to it even though they\u2019ve already paid to do so", "modifiers": {"italic": true}}, {"text": ".", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Damn it, I can\u2019t even properly describe how massive that failure is. Holy crap. Edsel, move over, this will be one for the history books.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "And now you\u2019re telling me that there are people who are convinced that consumers will start buying AI slop because they want AI to succeed. Have those people ever visited the real world?", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

question.title: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "Why can an AI model achieve high overall accuracy but still be considered untrustworthy or unethical?", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

answer.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "First, let me distinguish between AI and large language models (\u201cLLMs\u201d). LLMs are one among many tools that utilize AI. But they\u2019re arguably the highest-profile tool, at least among the general public. So some people in the general public tend to not distinguish between AI and LLMs.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "I\u2019ll talk about LLMs in a sec, but let me emphasize that other AI tools do not suffer from the same drawbacks as LLMs. Take game-playing AI, for example. One of the recent watershed moments in chess was the release of an AI-based chess engine called Alpha Zero.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Before Alpha Zero, chess engines were programmed by people who knew how to play chess. The humans would bake in their own knowledge about the game, and then program the computer to execute plans developed from that knowledge. Because computers were way better at calculating than humans, these chess engines were already stronger than any human on Earth.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "But Alpha Zero was different. It was not programmed with any ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "a priori ", "modifiers": {"italic": true}}, {"text": "chess knowledge except the rules of the game. It discovered everything it needed to know about chess on its own, by playing billions of games against itself and identifying patterns that emerged.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "And Alpha Zero was not only better than any human, it was also better than any of the previously-developed chess engines at the time. Consistently.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "I emphasize \u201cconsistently,\u201d to anchor back to the question. Alpha Zero is not seen as \u201cuntrustworthy.\u201d If I had to bet my life on the outcome of a match between Alpha Zero and any human in history, I would have absolutely no anxiety betting on Alpha Zero. Even in a a 100 or a 1,000 game match of Alpha Zero vs. any human in history, Alpha Zero wouldn\u2019t lose a single game. \u201cHallucinations\u201d aren\u2019t a thing in this part of the AI pond.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "horizontal-rule", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Which brings me to LLMs. LLMs hallucinate a lot, because the potential to do so is inherently in their nature. LLMs are trained on massive amounts of text. They are programmed to recognize patterns that are inherent in that text. Then, given a certain amount of text (which is the prompt), they predict what the rest of the text \u201cshould\u201d look like, based on the patterns they recognized in the training data.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Note that none of this involves any understanding. When it incorporates a sentence like \u201clobsters live in the ocean\u201d from its training data into its trained model, it doesn\u2019t understand what a lobster is, what an ocean is, or what it means for a thing to live somewhere. It just knows that \u201cocean\u201d is a good way to finish the phrase \u201clobsters live in the ___\u201d. It knows that \u201clobsters\u201d is an answer that fits in \u201c___ live in the ocean.\u201d", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Not only does it not know what a lobster or an ocean is, there\u2019s no feedback in the training phase. It doesn\u2019t recognize a pattern during training, then get additional input from somewhere (like a human) that says \u201cno; that pattern is a bad pattern.\u201d This, BTW, is in contrast to game-playing AIs. Game-playing AIs get feedback in the form of winning or losing games during training.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "This approach is bound to produce hallucinations, if only because (a) the whole thing is probabilistic in nature, and (b) there\u2019s no \u201creality check\u201d on an output based on understanding what the output means.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

question.title: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "Have the AI LLM vendors weaponized the term \"hallucinate\" so that it is now the equivalent to the politicians face saving retort \"it was a joke\"?", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

answer.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "First of all, there is incentive for politicians to lie. There is no incentive for LLMs to hallucinate. They are in no way trying to sneak in something untruthful because it somehow advances their agenda. (if they actually do that, say they have been given an intentional bias, that is not referred to as a hallucination)", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Hallucinations (which honestly, would be better named \u201cconfabulations\u201d) are genuine errors. So that\u2019s a pretty big difference.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Nobody is claiming hallucinations are a good thing. The LLM vendors would have their LLMs not hallucinate if it was possible. My experience is they do it an awful lot less than they used to, especially if you use the \u201cthinking\u201d models, the ones that write stuff down in a scratchpad area before composing the final answer.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "And I think you are weaponizing the word \u201cweaponizing\u201d. If you want to call it a \u201clame excuse,\u201d ok, but I don\u2019t see this as weaponizing, nor that it is in any way claiming that it \u201cmeant to do it,\u201d which differentiates it from \u201cit was a joke.\u201d", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "", "modifiers": {"embed": {"url": "https://youtu.be/urnRVr1P2bc?t=65"}}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "yt-embed", "is_rtl": false}]}

question.title: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "Why do so many people keep saying the \u201cAI Bubble\u201d is going to \u201cpop\u201d, when it\u2019s pretty obvious that the current models are merely prototypes for the real breakthroughs?", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

answer.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "Bubbles don\u2019t necessarily mean that the technology/goods/services at issue are worthless/trash, just that the valuations of the companies providing them have grown beyond merely being aggressive to the point of being irrational. Or, to put it another way, there is way too much money \u201cin\u201d the companies relative to the profits that will realistically come \u201cout\u201d of them in an acceptable amount of time.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Those of us of a certain age can all remember the Dot Com Bubble. The internet obviously ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "did", "modifiers": {"italic": true}}, {"text": " massively change society and created trillions of dollars in new wealth, so it wasn\u2019t like this then-new technology was pure hype or a flash in the pan. But because investors were so hyped on the transformative power of the internet, they poured enormous sums of money into low-margin (or even \u201cwe\u2019ll figure out how to make a profit later\u201d), poorly-run businesses simply because the companies were web-based. You had companies with valuations in the hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars in spite of the fact that they were burning money and had no coherent path to profitability, or indeed, could ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "never", "modifiers": {"italic": true}}, {"text": " support their stratospheric valuations. Dog shit plus the internet still equals dog shit, in other words, no matter how much people wanted that not to be true. Indeed, many people, if they were being honest, knew that internet stocks were overpriced, but they were relying on the \u201cgreater fool strategy,\u201d i.e., that while they recognize they\u2019re holding something that\u2019s likely overpriced, as long as there\u2019s some sucker out there willing to buy it at a premium, everything will work out OK. This approach works until, of course, it doesn\u2019t and you find yourself as the last fool in the chain. Once people awoke from their trances and scrutinized the stocks at issue ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "as businesses", "modifiers": {"italic": true}}, {"text": " as opposed to mere vehicles to \u201cinvest in the internet,\u201d the house of cards fell apart and there was a rash of bankruptcies.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Another common story is that when a new technology/service requires a ton of \u201cbuild out,\u201d something useful may be the end result, but the ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "cost", "modifiers": {"italic": true}}, {"text": " of getting to that end point proves ruinous because the timeline is too long/expensive for investors. Fiber optic networks, for example, are benefitting everyone reading this post, but a lot of the companies that built out said networks went bankrupt, because while they created something useful, they spent a ton of money doing so and weren\u2019t able to get profitable in time or the expected profits turned out to be far less than anticipated. That\u2019s a different kind of bubble.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "AI is one of the most capital-intensive undertakings of all time. That is, the sunk cost for AI is enormous - already in the trillions of dollars - with expected spending of more than $1 trillion per year for the foreseeable future. No one is suggesting that AI isn\u2019t useful - it already is showing utility - or that, as you note, \u201creal breakthroughs\u201d might be just around the corner. However, money is finite: investors who have invested in AI are happy right now even though companies aren\u2019t making money because the optimistic climate is still propelling values upward. But at ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "some", "modifiers": {"italic": true}}, {"text": " point, one of two things (or both) will happen: either (a) investors will balk at giving ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "yet more", "modifiers": {"italic": true}}, {"text": " trillions of dollars for build-out costs and/or (b) the optimistic climate goes away for some reason (maybe there\u2019s a recession, maybe one of those \u201cbreakthroughs\u201d your question hypothesizes changes the AI business model, etc.) and all of a sudden, people are negative on high-cost, money-losing businesses and seek to sell. That\u2019s when the bubble pops. Again, that doesn\u2019t mean that AI is worthless, just that some early-stage companies that are flying high today may not be around as the technology \u201cgrows up.\u201d", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

question.title: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "What are some examples of companies that are being remade by AI?", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

answer.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "The companies being remade by AI are not always the ones shouting about AI the loudest.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "A better sign is when the way people actually work starts changing.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Take a company running a large ERP or CRM system.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "A few years ago, an employee might spend part of the day checking records, moving information between systems, preparing reports, validating data or chasing down exceptions.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Now imagine some of that work being handled quietly by AI agents in the background.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The employee doesn't necessarily open ChatGPT or type a prompt.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The AI simply notices that something needs checking, pulls the relevant information, prepares the next step and brings a person in when a decision actually needs judgment.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "That, to me, is a much bigger transformation than adding a chatbot to a website.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "You can already see the same pattern in different parts of a business.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "In finance, AI can help with reconciliation and spotting unusual transactions.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "In customer service, it can bring together customer history before an agent responds.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "In sales, it can summarize account activity and keep CRM records updated.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "In operations, it can help with reporting, maintenance, inventory or repetitive ERP tasks.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "None of those examples sound particularly futuristic.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "But that's probably the point.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The most important AI changes inside companies may end up looking quite boring from the outside.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "A process that used to require eight manual steps might now require two.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "A report that took three hours to prepare might be ready before the meeting starts.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "An employee who spent half the morning searching for information might get the context they need immediately.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Multiply those small changes across hundreds of employees and thousands of transactions, and the company starts operating differently.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "That's when I'd say AI is actually remaking a business.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "There is also a big difference between using AI and building the business around AI assisted ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "workflows", "modifiers": {"bold": true}}, {"text": ".", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, question.title: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "How do AI headshot generators work, and are they worth it?", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

answer.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "Two separate questions, and the second one depends on what you need the photo for.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "How they work: you upload somewhere between 6 and 15 photos, and the platform briefly fine tunes an image generation model on your face. It maps facial geometry first, the distances between your eyes, the jawline, the shape of your nose and a few hundred other landmarks, and that becomes the anchor the model generates against. Then it fine tunes on your actual photos so it picks up skin texture, hair, freckles, facial hair, the things that make the output look like you rather than a generic person with your bone structure.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Generation swaps everything around your face: studio lighting, neutral background, business attire. The better platforms then run post processing to catch the usual artifacts, unnatural edges, inconsistent lighting, skin tone drift.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The single biggest factor in your output is your input photos. Natural light, several angles, no filters, no sunglasses, and photos taken on different days rather than fifteen near identical frames from one session. Near duplicates make the model overfit to one look and the results get stiff.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Whether it is worth it depends on the job. For a LinkedIn photo, a corporate directory or a conference speaker page, yes, pretty clearly. It is $29 to $39 against $150 to $400 for a session, you get 40 to 200 variations instead of 3 to 10 selects, and independent testing puts recruiters at roughly 73 percent unable to tell the difference. LinkedIn's circular crop also hides the corners, which is where artifacts usually show up.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Where it is not worth it: if your face is part of your brand. Actors, executives whose photo runs in press, anyone who needs an environmental portrait or a genuine expression caught in the moment. A generator cannot produce a real reaction, only a plausible one.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The part most people skip is the privacy question. Your face is biometric data, and retention policies vary a lot. Some platforms delete the fine tuned model within 48 hours. Some keep your data 30 days so you can re-download. A few hold it indefinitely unless you ask. If you are in the EU, GDPR applies, and Illinois, Texas and Washington each have their own biometric laws. Reading the retention section before you upload takes two minutes and is the only part of this that is hard to undo.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}
